issue: `_cleanup_tar_process` sends terminate and kill only to the tar pid, although `start_new_session=True` gives tar its own process group (tar_archive.py:502, tar_archive.py:527-533). On Linux, GNU tar `-z` forks gzip, which inherits the stderr pipe. So the post-kill `process.communicate()` with no timeout (tar_archive.py:533) waits for gzip to exit, not the bounded wait promised in the PRD Risks section. `os.killpg` would close this gap
reason: Reviewed design explicitly limits v1 to the direct child; descendant-held-pipe cleanup is a recorded non-blocker.

issue: Two new system-tar behaviours have no test. First, removing the cancel check between fsync/chmod and `os.replace` (tar_archive.py:475) breaks no test: no test sets the event after `communicate` returns, and the Python engine has `test_cancel_cleans_when_requested_during_fsync` but the system engine has no counterpart. Second, the design's "any other exception after spawn must stop/reap the live child before returning the invocation-failure fallback" is untested: no test makes `communicate` raise `OSError` while `poll()` is None

The PRD says `cancel` goes to every capability call, but `Runner._plan` calls `capability.plan(**call_kwargs)` without it (runner.py:157-164). This is harmless while plan only reads metadata, but it does not match the PRD wording, and a future capability whose plan does I/O could not be cancelled

The Capability protocol docstring still says the runner lets FatalError through and turns only other exceptions into failed steps (capabilities/__init__.py:21-24). `_run_instance` now turns a worker FatalError into a failed step (runner.py:208, asserted by test_failure_isolated_from_other_workers). The code follows the PRD; the docstring is out of date

Ctrl-C has no way out when a writer is slow to see `cancel`. `_walk_tree` and `_select_items` check `cancel` only after the whole walk (tar_archive.py:183-184), and the Python engine checks only between members. Every repeated Ctrl-C is swallowed (runner.py:122, runner.py:136, cli.py:50, cli.py:248), so a large or stalled source tree keeps the process alive until SIGTERM or SIGKILL. The docs mention only the per-member delay (docs/source/tools/backup.rst:43-44)

`_report_steps` re-renders the pending step after any KeyboardInterrupt. That includes one that lands after `_report_step` printed and the counter went up but before `pending = None` (cli.py:40-47). A Ctrl-C at that moment prints the step twice and counts it twice in the summary

Runner has public members beyond the PRD's exports (`Runner(cfg, dry_run, jobs)`, `Runner.interrupted`): `request_cancel()` and `cancelled_names` (runner.py:45, runner.py:47). The CLI needs them to handle Ctrl-C during rendering and to name unfinished instances, so they add no new feature, but they are undocumented API
`_run_instance` materializes the capability iterator, so a later `ArchiveCancelled` or exception throws away earlier successful results from a multi-result capability
`start_new_session=True` takes tar out of the terminal's process group. SIGHUP (terminal close) or SIGTERM to Python orphans a running tar, which keeps writing and leaves a `.tmp` sibling

`KeyboardInterrupt` is an asynchronous exception, so a few bytecode positions stay outside the handlers: generator entry before `run`'s try, and the `_execute` loop back-edge after the inner try. An interrupt there escapes the generator. Unyielded results are then dropped and unsubmitted names are left out of `cancelled_names` ("interrupted: no unfinished instances")
No test interrupts `_shutdown`'s join a second time to show the cleanup still completes after repeated Ctrl-C
